pr_body:
This implements `INLINESTATS`. Most of the heavy lifting is done by `LOOKUP`, with this change mostly adding a new abstraction to logical plans, an interface I'm calling `Phased`. Implementing this interface allows a logical plan node to cut the query into phases. `INLINESTATS` implements it by asking for a "first phase" that's the same query, up to `INLINESTATS`, but with `INLINESTATS` replaced with `STATS`. The next phase replaces the `INLINESTATS` with a hash join on the results of the first phase.

So, this query:
```
FROM foo
| EVAL bar = a * b
| INLINESTATS m = MAX(bar) BY b
| WHERE m = bar
| LIMIT 1
```

gets split into
```
FROM foo
| EVAL bar = a * b
| STATS m = MAX(bar) BY b
```

followed by
```
FROM foo
| EVAL bar = a * b
| LOOKUP (results of m = MAX(bar) BY b) ON b
| WHERE m = bar
| LIMIT 1
```


Here's an example of the syntax:
```
$ curl -k -XDELETE -u'elastic:password' 'http://localhost:9200/test'
$ for a in {0..99}; do
    echo -n $a
    rm -f /tmp/bulk
    for b in {0..999}; do
        echo '{"index": {}}' >> /tmp/bulk
        echo '{"a": '$a', "b": '$b'}' >> /tmp/bulk
    done
    curl -s -k -XPOST -u'elastic:password' -HContent-Type:application/json 'http://localhost:9200/test/_bulk?pretty' --data-binary @/tmp/bulk | grep errors
done
$ curl -s -k -XPOST -u'elastic:password' -HContent-Type:application/json 'http://localhost:9200/test/_forcemerge?max_num_segments=1&pretty'
$ curl -s -k -XPOST -u'elastic:password' -HContent-Type:application/json 'http://localhost:9200/test/_refresh?pretty'
$ curl -k -XPOST -u'elastic:password' -HContent-Type:application/json http://localhost:9200/_query?pretty -d'{
    "query": "FROM test | INLINESTATS m=MAX(a * b) BY b | WHERE m == a * b | SORT a DESC, b DESC | LIMIT 1",
    "profile": true
}'
{
  "columns" : [
    {
      "name" : "a",
      "type" : "long"
    },
    {
      "name" : "b",
      "type" : "long"
    },
    {
      "name" : "m",
      "type" : "long"
    }
  ],
  "values" : [
    [
      99,
      999,
      98901
    ]
```

Closes #107589

This is riddled with NOCOMMITs, as any good prototype deserves to be.

It's also not clear that this is the right way to go about this. I mean, cutting the request into two *is* the right way to do it, I think. The reworking of the callbacks to make that possible seems like the sane way to do that.

But from a planning side, this is an "interesting" choice. We analyze the `INLINESTATS` call, but then don't run the optimizer on it at all - that seems bad. OTOH, we *do* run the optimizer on the two halves of the query. That seems good.

Apparently the additioinal [SORT](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/109583/commits/887b9ce6643a2076f94beb519bdd8f2025375156#diff-a5ed793b796c14ec1f92807242ff2376e16888c8cf7627a4f6a8f57f23ed843aR309) makes it work.


I was wondering about **something** else yesterday, but I _think_ that **something** is somewhat related to [this TODO](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/109583/files#diff-2c689d9c0606d310fd36a603064f43cb4b23d356f08983fbdb98c65e76e6919dR1124). **Why is this "split" of plans done after the analysis and not after the logical optimization?**

I am asking this because any potential optimizations that let things pass through a stats/inlinestats do not happen anymore. I quickly looked over the logical optimization rules:
- PropagateEvalFoldables should do its job over Aggregates as well in the very near future, but the way the plans are split now, this rule will have a per-sub-plan wide visibility, but I think it should have a per-root-plan wide visibility somehow
- SkipQueryOnLimitZero might need to adapt and "duplicate" the `limit 0` to all the descending plans, to avoid unnecessary operations (joins essentially), if the end result will be thrown away
- PushDownAndCombineFilters can push down some filters past aggregates. This won't happen anymore for `inlinestats`.
- maybe others, I checked only a few of them.

Also, related to the ["experimental" nature of `inlinestats`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/109583/files#r1679306373), there may be some unforeseen consequences of having split plans with regards to the optimizer. Some of these are definitely non breaking (the query returns no error and no exception) and are strictly optimizations, but some of them may result in inconsistencies (not all the optimization rules are in fact optimizations) and return an exception or error that we didn't expect.
The high level of uncertainty here is the one that's most concerning imo. Also, the amount of work for the followups is unknown to me.

Leaving all these aside, this is an awesome feature, highly sought-after and it should be taken for a test drive.

> Hey, I just realized: there's likely a whole host of weird edge cases that can happen due to the multi-phase approach:
> 
>     * field caps response might not be up to date anymore, resp.

Mappings in ES can only change in a way that makes them "bigger". So I think this is *mostly* safe.

> 
>     * index/enrich resolution might become invalid between first and second phase (indices might be deleted or updated)

I think both of these are problems between field caps and runtime too. I *think* these are ok and we have to mostly think about error messages.

Except deleting an index. That one we have a solution for. Or, rather, we *can* have a solution for it. See below on data change.

> 
>     * data nodes might crash or restart

Yeah. At the moment we just lose queries then. Same for _search.

>     * the first phase's result might cause CBE or OOM

Same as above. I do want to check on the error messages for circuit breaker exceptions from a phase though.
> 
>     * data is ingested at a fast pace - at what point do we consider the inconsistency between the phases' results inacceptable?

This is something I stuck in a follow-up. _search has a mechanism where it keeps the `IndexReader` open between phases. We might wish to use that mechanism too. Especially if we want to use `Phased` to make a `FetchPhase`. But there are downsides. We could leave a lot of file handles open, for example. And indices can't be deleted between request. But you get the same view for both requests. The same documents. Even deleted documents aren't deleted in your view. It's quite repeatable-read.

I think we should think about adopting this but I want to hold it until a follow up. Because I think we have something useful here even if we don't turn it on. But I think deciding what to do here is a blocker for GA.

> **Why is this "split" of plans done after the analysis and not after the logical optimization?**

I'm 99% sure we have to split after analysis. But we could split after logical optimization - but if we do, I think we need to rerun logical optimization on the new plans. The `firstPhase` and the combined results. I think there's important stuff that can happen there.

As to the partial/incomplete nature of things - my hope was that by firing the sub-queries through the same stack of optimizations it would be safe. So long as each sub-plan is a valid LogicalPlan. In this case the the "firstPhase" is a normal ES query without the implicit `LIMIT`. And the last phase is pretty much a normal query with a `LOOKUP` in it. The case where we support the non-grouped merge is a bit unique, but not too different.
